entities.summary:
The Aeacidae were the royal dynasty of Epirus (northwestern Greece/Albania), claiming divine descent from Aeacus (grandson of Zeus and grandfather of Achilles), making them one of antiquity's most prestigious royal lineages. The dynasty produced two historically significant figures: Pyrrhus of Epirus (r. 306-272 BCE), one of antiquity's greatest commanders, whose campaigns against Rome introduced the term 'Pyrrhic victory'; and Alexander I of Epirus (r. 342-331 BCE), who campaigned in Italy before Alexander the Great's Eastern campaigns.

Pyrrhus of Epirus was considered by contemporaries — including Hannibal — to be the greatest general of antiquity after Alexander the Great. Pyrrhus's campaigns in Macedon, Thessaly, and his Italian campaigns (280-275 BCE) fighting against Rome and the Samnites demonstrated tactical brilliance. His victories at Heraclea (280 BCE) and Asculum (279 BCE) inflicted heavy Roman losses but at such high cost to his own army that 'another such victory and we are undone' entered language as the Pyrrhic victory concept.

Alexander I of Epirus, Pyrrhus's predecessor and uncle, crossed to Italy in 334 BCE — two years before Alexander the Great crossed into Asia — at the invitation of Tarentum (Taranto) fighting against the Lucanians and Samnites. He was killed in 331 BCE in Italy. The Aeacid dynasty's claim of Achilles' lineage made Epirus a culturally significant kingdom disproportionate to its small territory, connecting Greek heroic tradition to political legitimacy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Aeacidae dynasty's Pyrrhus of Epirus gave the world the concept of the 'Pyrrhic victory' — a military success so costly as to be defeat — making it the royal family whose military legacy permanently entered global vocabulary.
